summary: Tiny battery-powered devices on IEEE 802.15.4 radio links can form 6LoWPAN networks, but neither the radio standard nor the 6LoWPAN format says how multi-hop mesh routing should work. This informational RFC describes the problem and sets out routing requirements that take account of low power and other limits of such devices.

plainLanguage.summary: A 6LoWPAN is a network of small wireless devices, the kind that run on a coin battery and have a few kilobytes of memory. The radio standard and the packet format define how to carry IPv6 over these links, but neither of them says how a packet finds its way across a mesh of several hops. This RFC works out what a routing protocol for such a network has to achieve.

subtitle: What a routing protocol has to achieve in a network of tiny, battery-powered wireless devices.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 and the 6LoWPAN packet format say how to carry IPv6 over small radio links, but neither says how a packet finds its way across a mesh of several hops.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two places routing can happen, route-over at the IP layer and mesh-under below it, then lists eighteen requirements grouped by device properties, link properties, network characteristics, security, mesh-under forwarding and management.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document rather than a protocol. It exists so that the design of a 6LoWPAN routing protocol can be judged against stated requirements rather than against a particular implementation.

today: RFC 6606 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It is a requirements document rather than a protocol specification, and it was written to guide the design of routing protocols for 6LoWPANs rather than to describe one.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
6LoWPANs are formed by devices compatible with the IEEE 802.15.4 standard. Most LoWPAN devices are distinguished by their low bandwidth, short range, scarce memory capacity, limited processing capability and other attributes of inexpensive hardware. The characteristics of nodes participating in LoWPANs are those described in the 6LoWPAN problem statement and in the IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 document, which has specified how to carry IPv6 packets over IEEE 802.15.4 and similar networks.

IEEE 802.15.4 distinguishes two types of device, full-function devices and reduced-function devices, but that distinction rests on some features of the MAC layer that are not always in use, so this document does not make it. Some 6LoWPAN nodes may limit themselves to the role of hosts only, while others may take part in routing, and this host/router distinction can correlate with the processing and storage capabilities of the device and the power available in a similar way to the full-function and reduced-function idea.

IEEE 802.15.4 networks support star and mesh topologies, but neither the IEEE 802.15.4 standard nor the 6LoWPAN format specification define how mesh topologies could be obtained and maintained. So 6LoWPAN formation and multi-hop routing can be supported either below the IP layer, in the adaptation layer or Logical Link Control, or at the IP layer. The document distinguishes the layer at which these services are performed by the terms route-over and mesh-under.

Several reasons are given for why existing IP routing protocols may not satisfy the needs of multi-hop routing in 6LoWPANs. Nodes have special types and roles, such as nodes drawing their power from primary batteries, power-affluent nodes, mains-powered and high-performance gateways and data aggregators, and routing protocols should support multiple device types and roles. More stringent requirements apply than in higher-performance networks: nodes have small memory sizes and low processing power and run on very limited power supplied by primary non-rechargeable batteries, with a few KB of RAM, a few dozen KB of ROM or flash memory and a few MHz of CPU being typical, and a node's lifetime is usually defined by the lifetime of its battery. Handling sleeping nodes is very critical, more so than in traditional ad hoc networks, because LoWPAN nodes might stay in sleep mode most of the time, and taking advantage of appropriate times for transmissions matters for efficient packet forwarding.

Routing in LoWPANs might also be a simpler problem than routing in higher-performance networks. LoWPANs might be either transit networks or stub networks, and under the assumption that LoWPANs are never transit networks, routing protocols may be drastically simplified, so this document focuses on the requirements for stub networks, with additional requirements possibly applying to transit networks. It might equally be a harder problem, because routing in LoWPANs requires power optimization and stable operation in lossy environments, and these requirements are not easily satisfiable all at once.

The 6LoWPAN problem statement mentions four requirements for routing protocols: low overhead on data packets, low routing overhead, minimal memory and computation requirements, and support for sleeping nodes with consideration of battery savings. This document turns those high-level requirements into more detailed ones. It states the routing requirements of 6LoWPAN applications in general, and does not imply that a single routing solution will be favourable for all applications; there is no requirement for different routing protocols to run simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: A 6LoWPAN is a network of small wireless devices, the kind that run on a coin battery and have a few kilobytes of memory. The radio standard and the packet format define how to carry IPv6 over these links, but neither of them says how a packet finds its way across a mesh of several hops. This RFC works out what a routing protocol for such a network has to achieve.

sections.title: Route-Over and Mesh-Under Routing
sections.content:
Apart from the wide variety of conceivable routing algorithms, routing in a 6LoWPAN can be performed in the IP layer, using a route-over approach, or below IP, as defined by the 6LoWPAN format document, using the mesh-under approach.

The route-over approach relies on IP routing and therefore supports routing over possibly various types of interconnected links. The mesh-under approach performs the multi-hop communication below the IP link. The most significant consequence of mesh-under is that the characteristics of IEEE 802.15.4 directly affect the 6LoWPAN routing mechanisms, including the use of 64-bit, or 16-bit short, link-layer addresses instead of IP addresses, so a 6LoWPAN would be seen as a single IP link.

The reference network model follows from that choice. For multi-hop communication in a route-over LoWPAN, all routers, meaning the 6LoWPAN Border Routers and the 6LoWPAN Routers, perform IP routing within the stub network, and the link-local scope covers the set of nodes within symmetric radio range of a node. In a mesh-under LoWPAN, the 6LBR is the only IPv6 router in the LoWPAN, so the IPv6 link-local scope includes all nodes in the LoWPAN, and a mesh-under mechanism must be provided to support multi-hop transmission.

There is no expectation of topologically based address assignment in a 6LoWPAN. Addresses are typically assigned on the basis of the EUI-64 addresses assigned at manufacturing time to nodes, or on the basis of a more or less random process assigning 16-bit MAC addresses to individual nodes. Within a 6LoWPAN there is therefore no opportunity for aggregation or summarization of IPv6 addresses beyond the sharing of one or more common prefixes.

Not all devices that are within radio range of each other need to be part of the same LoWPAN. Where multiple LoWPANs are formed with globally unique IPv6 addresses, and a device of one LoWPAN wants to communicate with a device of another, the normal IPv6 mechanisms are employed. For route-over, the IPv6 address of the target is set as the destination of the packets and the devices perform IP routing to the 6LBR. For mesh-under, there is one IP hop from the device to the 6LBR of its own LoWPAN, no matter how many radio hops apart they are.

In order to avoid packet fragmentation and the overhead for reassembly, routing packets should fit into a single IEEE 802.15.4 physical frame, and application data should not be expanded to an extent that it no longer fits.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to build it. With route-over, every router runs IP routing and the network behaves like a set of IP links. With mesh-under, only the border router speaks IP and the other nodes just relay frames by radio address, so the whole LoWPAN looks like one IP link to anything outside it.

sections.title: Scenario Parameters
sections.content:
The document notes that IP-based LoWPAN technology is still at an early stage of development, that the range of conceivable usage scenarios is tremendous, and that the numerous possible applications of sensor networks make it obvious that mesh topologies will be prevalent and robust routing a necessity. Research in sensor networking has produced a large variety of multi-hop routing algorithms, most of which focus on optimizing routing for specific application scenarios, realized using several modes of communication: flooding in very small networks, hierarchical routing, geographic routing and self-organizing coordinate routing. The parameters that follow can be used to describe specific scenarios in which candidate routing protocols could be evaluated.

Network properties. The number of devices, the density and the network diameter usually affect the routing state directly, for example the number of entries in a routing table or neighbour list, and in large and dense networks policies must be applied for discarding low-quality and stale routing entries in order to prevent memory overflow. Connectivity can range from always connected to rarely connected, which poses great challenges for dynamic route discovery. Dynamicity, including mobility, matters because location changes cause route changes and nodes may be introduced into and removed from a LoWPAN. Deployment can scatter nodes randomly or organize them, at once or as an iterative process. The spatial distribution of nodes and gateways affects connectivity, congestion and available data rate: assuming a random spatial distribution, an average of 7 neighbours per node are required for approximately 95% network connectivity, and 10 neighbours per node are needed for 99% connectivity. Traffic patterns, topology and applications decide which routing type is most efficient, with mechanisms such as data-centric, event-driven, address-centric and geographic routing. Classes of service may be needed where applications of different criticality share one LoWPAN. Security matters because LoWPANs may carry sensitive information, and secured messages cause overhead and affect power consumption.

Node parameters. Processing speed and memory size define the maximum size of the routing state and the maximum complexity of its processing. Power consumption and power source affect the selection of paths that optimize network lifetime. Transmission range affects routing, because a high transmission range may cause a dense network, which results in more direct neighbours of a node, higher connectivity and a larger routing state. Traffic pattern affects routing, since highly loaded nodes, whether because they are the source of packets or because they forward them, may contribute to higher delivery delays and may consume more energy than lightly loaded nodes.

Link parameters. These apply to IEEE 802.15.4 legacy mode, without making use of improved modulation schemes. The maximum user data throughput of a bulk data transmission between a single sender and a single receiver through an unslotted IEEE 802.15.4 2.4 GHz channel in ideal conditions is 151.6 kbit/s with 16-bit MAC addresses in unreliable mode, 139.0 kbit/s with 16-bit MAC addresses in reliable mode, 135.6 kbit/s with 64-bit MAC addresses in unreliable mode and 124.4 kbit/s with 64-bit MAC addresses in reliable mode. The 915 MHz band gives 31.1, 28.6, 27.8 and 25.6 kbit/s for the same four cases, and the 868 MHz band gives 15.5, 14.3, 13.9 and 12.8 kbit/s. Latency ranges for a frame transmission on the 2.4 GHz channel are [1.92 ms, 6.02 ms] for 16-bit addresses in unreliable mode, [2.46 ms, 6.56 ms] for 16-bit addresses in reliable mode, [2.75 ms, 6.02 ms] for 64-bit addresses in unreliable mode and [3.30 ms, 6.56 ms] for 64-bit addresses in reliable mode; on the 868 MHz band the ranges are [11.7 ms, 58.7 ms], [16.7 ms, 63.7 ms], [17.9 ms, 58.7 ms] and [22.9 ms, 63.7 ms]. The RFC notes that multi-criteria routing may be too expensive for 6LoWPAN nodes, so single-criteria metrics can be selected to suit the environment or application.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the things a test should state about a deployment: how many devices, how dense, how they move, how much battery, how far they can hear, and what the radio can carry. These are the knobs a candidate protocol is measured against.

sections.title: The Routing Requirements
sections.content:
Section 5 states eighteen requirements in six groups. The importance of each depends on the node type and the role the protocol is running on, and the requirements consider the presence of battery-powered nodes in LoWPANs.

Device properties. R01 says routing protocols should allow implementation with small code size and low routing state to fit typical node capacity: code size is bounded by available flash memory and the routing table is bounded by RAM size, possibly limiting it to less than 32 entries. The RAM size of LoWPAN nodes often ranges between 4 KB and 10 KB, with 2 KB minimum, and program flash memory normally consists of 48 KB to 128 KB; code should fit within no more than 48 KB to 128 KB of flash including at least a few tens of KB of application code, and there should be at least one mode of operation that can function with 32 forwarding entries or less. R02 says routing protocols should cause minimal power consumption by efficiently using control packets, minimizing expensive IP multicast which causes link broadcast to the entire LoWPAN, and by efficiently routing data packets, because radio communication is by far the dominant factor of power consumption compared with computational operations or taking sensor samples.

Link properties. R03 says routing protocol control messages should not exceed a single IEEE 802.15.4 frame size, to avoid packet fragmentation and the overhead for reassembly: the standard specifies an MTU of 127 bytes, yielding about 80 octets of actual MAC payload with security enabled, some of which is taken for the typically compressed IP header. R04 says the design must consider that packets are to be delivered with sufficient probability according to application requirements: some non-critical industrial monitoring applications may tolerate a successful delivery ratio of less than 90% with hours of latency, in other cases a delivery ratio of 99.9% is required, and in building automation application-layer errors must be below 0.01%. R05 says the design must consider the latency requirements of applications and the IEEE 802.15.4 link latency characteristics, which range from a few hundred milliseconds to minutes depending on the application: real-time building automation usually needs response times below 500 ms, forced-entry security alerts must be routed to one or more devices within 5 seconds, and industrial control loops can have latency requirements as low as 100 ms. R06 says routing protocols should be robust to dynamic loss caused by link failure or device unavailability in the short term, approximately 30 ms. R07 says they should be designed to operate correctly in the presence of link asymmetry, where the probability of successful transmission between two nodes is significantly higher in one direction than in the other.

6LoWPAN characteristics. R08 says the design should take into account that some nodes may be unresponsive during certain intervals because of periodic hibernation: many nodes might periodically disable their transceiver activity, and feedback from the lower IEEE 802.15.4 layer may be used to enhance power awareness. CC1000-based nodes must operate at a duty cycle of approximately 2% to survive for one year from an idealized AA battery source, and for home automation a duty cycle lower than 1% is suggested. R09 says the routing metric should provide flexibility with respect to the inputs provided by the lower layers and other measures to optimize path selection, considering energy balance and link qualities; nodes installed with mains power must be considered as relay points for a prominent role in packet delivery, and routing protocols must know the power constraints of the nodes, since simple hop-count-only mechanisms may be inefficient in 6LoWPANs. R10 says routing protocols should achieve both scalability, from a few nodes to maybe millions, and minimal use of system resources: home automation is envisioned to need 250 devices, metropolitan-scale sensor networks must cluster sensing nodes into regions of the order of 10^2 to 10^4 nodes, and in large networks the number of routers must be smaller than the number of hosts. R11 says route repair and its control messages should not harm overall energy consumption. R12 says routing protocols should allow for dynamically adaptive topologies and mobile nodes, with route maintenance keeping in mind a minimal routing state and message overhead; dynamic association and disassociation must be supported in 6LoWPANs. R13 says a routing protocol should support various traffic patterns, point-to-point, point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-point, while avoiding excessive multicast traffic.

Security. R14 says routing protocols must support confidentiality, authentication and integrity services as required for secure delivery of control messages. Security is important but costly, and public key cryptography primitives are typically avoided as being too expensive, as are heavyweight conventional encryption methods. It becomes questionable whether 6LoWPAN devices can support IPsec as it is, because IPsec is computationally expensive given the power constraints and limited processing capability of the devices, and because IKEv2 messaging will not work well in 6LoWPANs where the amount of signalling should be minimized, and IPsec adds another header to every packet. A 6LoWPAN may therefore need to define its own keying management methods with minimum overhead in packet size and in the number of signalling messages, with security requested at the application layer where needed. If IEEE 802.15.4 security is used, no other protection is needed for Neighbor Discovery as long as no node becomes compromised. The IEEE 802.15.4 MAC provides an AES-based security mechanism, and in the worst case in terms of overhead that mechanism consumes 21 bytes of MAC payload. IEEE 802.15.4 does not specify protection for acknowledgment frames, so acknowledgments cannot be relied upon, and in applications that require high security the routing protocol must not exploit feedback from acknowledgments.

Mesh-under forwarding and management. R15 says mesh-under requires the development of a routing protocol operating below IP, which must support 16-bit short and 64-bit extended MAC addresses. R16 says LoWPAN nodes should avoid sending separate 'Hello' messages for neighbour discovery and maintenance, and may instead use link-layer mechanisms such as acknowledgments, since any frame received by a node can serve as an input for evaluating connectivity. R17 says that if the routing protocol functionality includes enabling IP multicast, it may employ structure in the network for efficient distribution in order to minimize link-layer broadcast. R18 says a 6LoWPAN routing protocol should be designed according to the guidelines for operations and management stated in RFC 5706, since options and parameters should be configured or negotiated dynamically rather than manually, and the protocol should allow monitoring of the status or value of its parameters and data structures such as routing table entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements all come back to the same three limits: the battery, the few kilobytes of memory, and the small frame. A protocol has to fit in those, has to survive links that drop packets in one direction more than the other, and has to cope with nodes that switch their radio off for long stretches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security issues are described in Section 5.4, and the security considerations in the 6LoWPAN problem statement, in the IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 document and in the generic threats to routing protocols document apply as well.

The use of wireless links renders a 6LoWPAN susceptible to attacks, as any other wireless network. In outdoor 6LoWPANs, the physical exposure of the nodes allows an adversary to capture, clone or tamper with the devices. In ad hoc 6LoWPANs that are dynamic in both their topology and node memberships, a static security configuration does not suffice: spoofed, altered or replayed routing information might occur, while multihopping could delay the detection and treatment of attacks.

The specification expects that the link layer is sufficiently protected, either by physical or IP security for the backbone link, or with MAC-sublayer cryptography. Link-layer encryption and authentication may not be sufficient to provide confidentiality, authentication, integrity and freshness to both data and routing protocol packets, and time synchronization, self-organization and secure localization for multi-hop routing are also critical to support. For secure routing protocol operation it may be necessary to consider authenticated broadcast and multicast and bidirectional link verification. Secure end-to-end data delivery can be assisted by the routing protocol, for example through multi-path routing to prevent selective forwarding, but 6LoWPANs already have high resource constraints, so the 6LBR and the LoWPAN nodes may require different security solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless links are easy to attack. An attacker who can reach the devices can capture, clone or tamper with them, and a mesh makes it slower to notice that routing information has been altered. The RFC assumes the link layer is protected, but says that on its own that is not enough for the routing messages.

viz.caption: THE SIX GROUPS OF REQUIREMENTS IN RFC 6606

items.title: Device properties
items.text: R01 and R02: small code size, low routing state, and minimal power consumption.

items.title: Link properties
items.text: R03 to R07: frame-sized control messages, delivery ratio, latency, short-term loss and link asymmetry.

items.title: 6LoWPAN characteristics
items.text: R08 to R13: hibernating nodes, routing metrics, scalability, route repair, mobility and traffic patterns.

items.title: Security
items.text: R14: confidentiality, authentication and integrity for control messages.

items.title: Mesh-under forwarding
items.text: R15 to R17: 16-bit and 64-bit MAC addresses, neighbour discovery without Hellos, and efficient multicast.

items.title: Management
items.text: R18: follow the operations and management guidelines, with dynamic configuration and monitoring.
